verdicts.claim: SQLite runs one automatically when a COMMIT leaves the WAL at 1000 pages or more ... and when the last connection to the database closes. SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'checkpoint automatically when the WAL file reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages. (The SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT compile-time option...)' and 'When the last connection to a database closes, that connection does one last checkpoint'

verdicts.claim: PASSIVE ... never calls the busy handler ... TRUNCATE ... truncates the WAL file to zero bytes just before it returns successfully
verdicts.evidence: v2 page: 'The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode' and TRUNCATE 'truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return'

verdicts.claim: A checkpoint must stop at the first WAL frame that is newer than the end mark of any current reader. It records its progress in the wal-index
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader... remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got'

verdicts.claim: journal_size_limit setting (default -1, meaning no limit; 0 means always truncate to the minimum size) ... must be set separately for each attached database
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: 'The default journal size limit is -1 (no limit)'; 'set the journal_size_limit to zero'; 'The size limit must be set separately for each attached database.'

verdicts.claim: PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=N ... Setting N to zero or a negative value turns auto-checkpointing off. Every automatic checkpoint runs in PASSIVE mode.
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: 'Setting the auto-checkpoint size to zero or a negative value turns auto-checkpointing off... All automatic checkpoints are PASSIVE.'

verdicts.claim: NOOP mode copies no frames. Its only use is to read the WAL size (*pnLog) and ... frames already checkpointed (*pnCkpt). After a successful TRUNCATE, both are 0
verdicts.evidence: v2 page: 'The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned ... *pnLog and *pnCkpt' and after TRUNCATE 'both *pnLog and *pnCkpt will be set to zero'

verdicts.claim: PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(MODE) returns one row with three columns ... busy 0/1 ... If the database is not in WAL mode, the second and third columns are -1
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: 'returns a single row with three integer columns. The first column is usually 0 but will be 1 if a RESTART or FULL or TRUNCATE checkpoint was blocked... The second and third column are -1' (for non-WAL)

verdicts.claim: Litestream keeps a long-running read transaction open so that no other process can checkpoint and restart the WAL. Litestream then runs the checkpoints
verdicts.evidence: how-it-works: 'It starts a long-running read transaction to prevent any other process from checkpointing and restarting the WAL file... manually calls out to SQLite to perform checkpoints'

verdicts.claim: Checkpoint starvation: if there is always at least one overlapping reader, no checkpoint completes and the WAL file grows without bound. 'reader gaps'
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound... ensuring that there are "reader gaps"'; readers 'might block' under RESTART/TRUNCATE

verdicts.claim: Every checkpoint takes an exclusive checkpoint lock ... returns SQLITE_BUSY at once and does not call the busy handler ... continues as a PASSIVE one
verdicts.evidence: v2 page: 'All calls obtain an exclusive "checkpoint" lock... SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked' and on busy-handler giving up 'proceeds ... in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE ... SQLITE_BUSY is returned'
